question: What does the Latin translation of the word pons mean?
explanation: The term pons translates to bridge because it connects different regions of the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h1)

question: The pons helps form the walls of which fluid-filled space in the brain?
explanation: The posterior surface of the pons directly forms the floor of the fourth ventricle. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h1)

question: Which major blood vessel runs vertically down the middle groove of the pons?
explanation: The basilar sulcus on the ventral surface of the pons provides a groove that cradles the basilar artery. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h2)

question: When looking at a cross-section, the internal structure of the pons is divided into which two main parts?
explanation: A horizontal cross-section divides the pons into the ventral basilar portion and the dorsal tegmentum. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h2)

question: Which cranial nerve has its primary nuclei located within the pons and controls the muscles used for chewing?
explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) exits from the pons and supplies the muscles of mastication. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h3)

question: An injury affecting the abducens nerve near the pons primarily impairs which movement?
explanation: The abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which pulls the eye outward away from the nose. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h3)

question: Which part of the respiratory center in the pons acts to limit inspiration and prevent lung overinflation?
explanation: The pneumotaxic center fine-tunes the respiratory rate by limiting inspiration. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h4)

question: What is the main result of damage to the apneustic center in the lower pons?
explanation: Without the inhibiting influence of the pneumotaxic center or when the apneustic center is damaged, breathing often features prolonged inspiratory gasps. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h4)

question: Locked-in syndrome is most commonly caused by damage to which brain structure?
explanation: A stroke in the basilar artery damaging the ventral pons disrupts motor pathways, causing complete paralysis while sparing consciousness. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h5)

question: A patient with a pontine stroke is completely paralyzed and mute, yet blinks and moves their eyes upward on command. What condition does this describe?
explanation: Locked-in syndrome leaves patients conscious and capable of vertical eye movements despite total motor paralysis. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h5)

question: Why is frequent airway assessment critical for patients with an acute pontine stroke?

options.A: Cranial nerve involvement can compromise swallowing and protective reflexes
options.B: The metabolic rate drops, reducing oxygen demand
options.C: Excessive mucus production occurs exclusively in brainstem injuries
options.D: Patients routinely develop sudden severe asthma attacks

explanation: Brainstem lesions often impair cranial nerves responsible for swallowing and airway protection, creating high aspiration risks. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h6)

question: What is the best initial nursing action when a patient with locked-in syndrome tries to communicate?

options.A: Insert a nasogastric tube immediately without further assessment
options.B: Administer sedatives to reduce patient frustration and anxiety
options.C: Establish a reliable eye-blink or vertical eye movement signaling system
options.D: Assume the patient is unconscious and limit verbal interaction

explanation: Since motor pathways are severed but cognition and vertical eye control remain intact, eye signals allow meaningful communication. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T20#GNS211_U3_T20_h6)
